title: Richer database context improves LLM-generated EHR phenotyping algorithms
authors: Ye, M.; Lee, H.; Gizlice, S.; Tobias, M.; O'Neil, S.; Pfaff, E.; Ahalt, S. C.
abstract: ObjectiveTo evaluate large language model (LLM) generation of type 2 diabetes (T2DM) phenotyping SQL and the effect of database implementation context. Materials and MethodsEight publicly accessible LLM-based systems generated SQL under progressively richer prompts using synthetic and University of North Carolina (UNC) Health electronic health record (EHR) data, both based on the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership (OMOP) model. Outputs were compared with the Electronic Medical Records and Genomics (eMERGE) T2DM reference phenotype using SQL executability, F1, positive predictive value (PPV), and recall. ResultsFewer than 55% of limited-context synthetic outputs and no limited-context UNC EHR outputs executed without modification. Detailed codebooks (L3) increased executability to 81.3% in synthetic OMOP and 100% in UNC EHR; adding sample rows (L4) increased synthetic executability to 100%. Limited-context recall was as low as 0.01, whereas high-context outputs achieved recall [≥]0.99 at synthetic L4 and >0.90 at UNC L3, although UNC PPV remained substantially lower than recall. At the highest available context levels, Beta F1 ranged from 0.72-0.99 in synthetic OMOP and 0.57-0.68 in UNC EHR; all UNC models exceeded the diagnosis-code baseline (F1=0.54). The top synthetic performer fell from F1=0.99 to 0.64 on UNC EHR. DiscussionRicher database context was associated with more consistent SQL executability and recall, while model rankings varied across datasets. ConclusionLLMs can generate clinically meaningful T2DM phenotyping SQL when provided with sufficient database context, but limited PPV in real-world data underscores the need for local validation.

infographic.key_insight: Richer database context improved LLM-generated type 2 diabetes phenotyping SQL executability and recall, but real-world precision remained limited.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Context-rich prompts may support EHR cohort identification for research, but generated phenotypes require local validation before use.
method: Eight publicly accessible LLM-based systems generated SQL with progressively richer database prompts.
Evaluated synthetic and UNC Health EHR datasets using the OMOP data model.
Compared outputs with the eMERGE reference phenotype using executability, F1, PPV, and recall.
infographic.evidence_signal: Detailed codebooks raised UNC SQL executability from 0% with limited context to 100%, while highest-context F1 ranged from 0.57–0.68 versus 0.54 for a diagnosis-code baseline.
infographic.watch_item: Performance did not transfer reliably: the top synthetic performer dropped from F1=0.99 to 0.64 on UNC EHR, where PPV remained substantially below recall.

title: Performance of a foundation model to generate thousands of predicted outcomes across multiple use cases
authors: Mischiati, M.; Vattis, K.; Gliklich, R.; Leavy, M. B.; Boussios, C.; Bandaria,, J.
abstract: BackgroundPredictive artificial intelligence (AI) models hold great promise for medical care. While many types of models have proliferated across healthcare and the life sciences, systematic, rapid generation of multi-condition predictions of diagnoses, future medical events and future clinical outcomes from a single foundation-model architecture remains rare. PhenOM(R) is a generative AI foundation model trained and validated on longitudinal medical-event data from more than 400 million patient records in the OM1 Real World Data Cloud (RWDC) and designed to complete predictive tasks for a broad array of medical diagnoses, events and clinical outcomes (collectively outcomes) at varying time intervals, currently up to five (5) years. This paper describes the implementation of PhenOM to complete a vast number of predictive tasks across clinical domains and outcomes. MethodsPhenOM was evaluated across four outcome categories (Future Risk, Screening, Care Opportunity, and Treatment Effect) in multiple domains spanning chronic disease, acute medical events, healthcare utilization, and rare and frequently undiagnosed conditions. Performance was assessed using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). Outcomes were defined within an eligible-population framework using standardized medical code sets (ICD-10, SNOMED, CPT, NDC, LOINC) unless outcomes could not be specified with an existing code. All benchmarks reported were derived from data excluded from training. ResultsAs of this publication, the single PhenOM model has been used to complete and validate thousands of predictive tasks covering more than 1,770 outcomes spanning most organ systems and clinical specialties, with new predictive tasks being validated each day. Overall, 80% of predictive tasks achieved AUROC of at least 0.70 and 30% achieved AUROC of at least 0.80. We present a sample of 177 of these tasks as examples that show the breadth of tasks the model can complete. Performance varied systematically by outcome and clinical domain. ConclusionsPhenOM demonstrates the ability to complete thousands of predictive tasks across clinical domains and outcomes at the individual patient level, without additional training. Outcomes include screening for undiagnosed conditions, predicting future conditions, medical events, effects of treatments, and assessing care opportunities. These can be ascertained at the individual patient and population levels. These findings support applications in individual and population health management, risk management, drug development, and real-world evidence generation, and establish a transparent, reproducible performance reference for a large-scale real-world predictive AI platform.

infographic.key_insight: A single PhenOM foundation model supported thousands of validated prediction tasks across more than 1,770 outcomes, with 80% of tasks achieving AUROC ≥0.70.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The model could support broad patient-level risk assessment across specialties, but clinical benefit was not established in the abstract.
method: Trained on longitudinal medical-event data from more than 400 million patient records.
Evaluated Future Risk, Screening, Care Opportunity, and Treatment Effect tasks.
Measured AUROC on data excluded from training, using standardized codes to define outcomes where possible.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 30% of tasks achieved AUROC ≥0.80 and presents 177 example tasks, with performance varying by outcome and clinical domain.
infographic.watch_item: AUROC alone does not establish calibration, clinical utility, or generalizability to new care settings.
infographic.paper_title: Performance of a foundation model to generate thousands of predicted outcomes across multiple use cases

title: MedMLX: On-Device Medical Imaging AI for Apple Silicon
authors: Sandoval, A.; Sandoval, J.; Saleem, A.
abstract: BackgroundMedical imaging research increasingly combines specialized artificial intelligence models for segmentation, detection, image synthesis and report generation. For three-dimensional CT and MRI, these workflows typically run on NVIDIA GPUs with substantial memory. On-device AI on widely available Apple Silicon computers could broaden access to these models for clinical researchers. These computers share a large memory pool between the CPU and GPU, which suits workflows that combine several models. However, few established imaging models run natively on Apple Silicon. Adapting a model to new hardware also requires verifying that its results match the original software. MethodsWe developed MedMLX, a collection of 21 established medical imaging models rewritten for Apple Silicon in MLX, Apples machine learning framework. The collection includes nnU-Net, TotalSegmentator, MedSAM2 and SAM 3. The models segment organs and tumors, detect lung nodules, generate synthetic images and draft radiology reports from CT, MRI, PET/CT, radiographs and endoscopic images. Using public cases from 11 imaging datasets, we compared the models results with those of the original software run on an Intel CPU and an NVIDIA GPU. Agreement required a Dice coefficient of at least 0.99 for every segmentation label and equivalent criteria for other outputs. We measured memory use and processing time on an Apple M1 Max computer with 64 GB of memory. ResultsMedMLX agreed with the original software in 211 of 212 comparisons. The single exception was a brain MRI segmentation. On this case, the original software itself gave different results on the two devices. We illustrated sequential workflows, including anatomical segmentation of a synthetic brain MRI and lesion synthesis guided by organ segmentation. With a memory-saving setting, 19 of the 21 models used less than 16 GB of memory. This setting reduced memory use by a median of 49% and increased processing time by a median of 13%. ConclusionsMedMLX enables on-device AI with established medical imaging models on Apple Silicon computers rather than specialized NVIDIA hardware. The models agree closely with the original software, and most need less than 16 GB of memory.

infographic.key_insight: MedMLX brings 21 established medical imaging AI models to Apple Silicon, matching original-software outputs in 211 of 212 comparisons.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Local execution could broaden researchers’ access to imaging AI without specialized NVIDIA hardware, but clinical performance was not established.
method: Reimplemented models in Apple’s MLX framework for segmentation, detection, image synthesis and report generation.
Compared outputs with original software running on an Intel CPU and NVIDIA GPU.
Measured memory use and processing time on an M1 Max with 64 GB memory.
infographic.evidence_signal: Testing used public cases from 11 datasets and required Dice ≥0.99 for every segmentation label; with memory-saving settings, 19 of 21 models used under 16 GB.
infographic.watch_item: Software-output agreement does not establish diagnostic accuracy or clinical safety; broader validation is needed before clinical deployment.
infographic.paper_title: MedMLX: On-Device Medical Imaging AI for Apple Silicon

title: Quantifying Localized Tumor-Infiltrating Lymphocytes by Deep Learning on H&E Images: Analytical Validation and Prognostic Value in Lung Adenocarcinoma
authors: Osinski, B. L.; Ingale, K.; Huang, A.; Terdich, B.; Muller, Y.; Joshi, R. P.; Miotto, R.; Jones, R. D.; Beaubier, N.; Sangli, C.
abstract: Tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) are a critical determinant of response to immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD). However, assessing the clinical utility of TIL quantification is challenging due to subjective manual scoring and differences in methodology, including some that may obscure localized immune responses critical to ICI response. Together, these issues limit our understanding of potential prognostic benefits of performing routine TIL quantification. Here, we present the "focal TIL score," an artificial intelligence-powered biomarker derived from routinely generated Hematoxylin & Eosin (H&E) pathology images which measures TIL density within tiles across the entire relevant tissue region in order to account for spatial heterogeneity of localized lymphocytic infiltration. Underlying this method are two deep learning models that ensure accurate, reproducible, and interpretable quantification: one for lymphocyte detection trained on IHC-derived ground truth, and one for segmentation of tumor and tumor-adjacent stroma region ("scorable region") trained on consensus pathologist annotations. We performed an analytical validation of the two models, demonstrating high overall performance: lymphocyte model concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) = 0.90, scorable region model Dice score = 0.87. We then performed a prognostic association study in a cohort of 685 ICI-treated LUAD patients and saw that, the focal TIL score was significantly associated with overall survival (HR=0.60, 95% CI 0.48-0.75, P<0.001), outperforming the standard biomarker PD-L1. Our findings show that quantifying the spatial intensity of immune infiltration, rather than the global average, provides a superior measure of the anti-tumor immune response. The accessibility and standardization associated with this approach may enable further studies and developments in precision oncology for LUAD.

infographic.key_insight: An AI-derived focal TIL score captures localized lymphocyte infiltration on routine H&E images and was associated with overall survival in ICI-treated lung adenocarcinoma.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The score may support accessible prognostic assessment, but this study does not establish its ability to predict benefit from immunotherapy.
method: Detect lymphocytes using a deep learning model trained on IHC-derived ground truth.
Segment tumor and adjacent stroma using a model trained on consensus pathologist annotations.
Quantify tile-level TIL density to capture spatially localized immune infiltration.
infographic.evidence_signal: Analytical validation yielded lymphocyte CCC 0.90 and segmentation Dice 0.87; in 685 ICI-treated patients, the score was associated with overall survival (HR 0.60, 95% CI 0.48–0.75; P<0.001) and reportedly outperformed PD-L1.
infographic.watch_item: Broader validation is needed before clinical use; an association within an ICI-treated cohort does not establish treatment-specific predictive value.
infographic.paper_title: Quantifying Localized Tumor-Infiltrating Lymphocytes by Deep Learning on H&E Images: Analytical Validation and Prognostic Value in Lung Adenocarcinoma

title: Evaluating the Incremental Value of AI-Derived ECG Features Beyond Automated ECG Reports and Clinical Data for 30-Day Mortality: A MIMIC-IV Cohort Study
authors: Park, S.-H.; Ji, Z.; Lewey, J.; Tsui, F.
abstract: Automated electrocardiogram (ECG) reports and clinical records already carry prognostic information, so the relevant question is what artificial intelligence (AI)-derived ECG waveform features add beyond these existing sources, and whether models with similar overall discrimination would prioritize the same patients for review. In linked Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV) data, we compared 15 prespecified ECG morphology measurements with features from a previously trained deep-learning model for 30-day all-cause mortality in the same 25,430 held-out patients (924 deaths). Both feature sets fed identical prediction models developed and evaluated with the same procedures; paired 95% confidence intervals quantify each difference, basic clinical history--age, recorded sex, and prior-diagnosis indicators--was held constant where indicated, and analyses are labelled prespecified or post hoc. The AI-feature model ranked 30-day mortality risk better than the morphology model (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.812 versus 0.737; +0.075, 95% CI +0.059 to +0.091), and the advantage persisted with basic clinical history (+0.053, +0.039 to +0.067). In post hoc comparisons with basic clinical history held constant, replacing the expanded automated report associated with the index ECG with AI features changed discrimination little (+0.0037, -0.0053 to +0.0126), and adding AI features to the report-based model yielded +0.0075 (-0.0005 to +0.0151); both intervals include zero. At a hypothetical fixed 5% review capacity, the prespecified ECG-only comparison identified 236 versus 163 subsequent deaths (AI features versus morphology measurements), and with basic clinical history the corresponding post hoc comparison identified 262 versus 221. In a separate post hoc comparison using separately refitted models, the AI-feature and expanded-report review lists captured 262 versus 261 subsequent deaths (paired difference +1, 95% CI -25 to +22), yet shared only 654 of their 1,272 flagged patients: similar totals, different patient lists. One-year transport to a Brazilian cohort absent from the model's earlier training retained the advantage over morphology measurements. These retrospective risk rankings measure prioritization, not prevented mortality: the advantage over richer routine reports was small and uncertain, and equal-capacity lists flagged different patients, so comparator strength and patient selection merit evaluation alongside discrimination before clinical use.

infographic.key_insight: AI-derived ECG features outperformed selected morphology measurements for 30-day mortality prediction but showed no clear discrimination gain over expanded automated ECG reports when basic clinical history was included.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Similar overall performance can conceal different patient prioritization: AI-feature and report-based models captured nearly identical numbers of deaths while sharing only about half of flagged patients.
method: Compared pretrained AI-derived ECG features with 15 prespecified ECG morphology measurements using identical prediction-model procedures.
Held age, recorded sex, and prior-diagnosis indicators constant in adjusted comparisons; assessed paired 95% confidence intervals.
Examined hypothetical 5% review lists and post hoc comparisons with expanded automated ECG reports.
infographic.evidence_signal: Among 25,430 held-out MIMIC-IV patients with 924 deaths, AI features improved AUROC over morphology by 0.075 (95% CI 0.059–0.091), but adding AI to reports plus clinical history yielded 0.0075 (−0.0005–0.0151).
infographic.watch_item: Report-based and review-list comparisons were post hoc, and hypothetical prioritization does not establish improved clinical outcomes.
infographic.paper_title: Evaluating the Incremental Value of AI-Derived ECG Features Beyond Automated ECG Reports and Clinical Data for 30-Day Mortality: A MIMIC-IV Cohort Study

title: Deep learning-based electrocardiographic differentiation of Takotsubo syndrome from acute anterior myocardial infarction: explainability, human-AI interaction, and a utilization bias hypothesis
authors: Kagawa, E.; Kato, M.; Hidaka, T.; Kunita, E.; Hironobe, N.; Matsui, S.; Kobayashi, Y.; Uotani, Y.; Teramoto, T.; Yoshii, K.; Okumoto, T.; Tani, M.; Dote, K.
abstract: BackgroundArtificial intelligence (AI) may improve electrocardiographic differentiation of Takotsubo syndrome from acute anterior ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), but its impact on human diagnostic performance, the added value of visual explanations, and differences by reader background and experience remain uncertain. MethodsUsing 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) images from two hospitals, we developed and externally validated an ensemble of three deep learning models after self-supervised pretraining and fine-tuning. The diagnostic task used ECGs recorded within 14 days after symptom onset, regardless of reperfusion status. We conducted a four-phase reader study. Phases 1-3 compared unaided interpretation, a reference sheet, and additional AI assistance. In Phase 4, readers evaluated a new ECG set after randomization to reference-sheet support alone, with AI predictions, or with AI predictions plus gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM) heatmaps. Diagnostic correctness was analyzed using generalized linear mixed-effects models. Exploratory analyses examined differences by cardiologist status and experience. ResultsDevelopment and external-validation cohorts, including healthy controls, comprised 832 and 95 participants, respectively. For Takotsubo-STEMI discrimination, external-validation accuracy was 0.914, with areas under the receiver operating characteristic and precision-recall curves of 0.970 and 0.984. Seventy healthcare providers completed the reader study. The estimated probability of correct diagnosis increased from 0.632 without assistance to 0.864 with AI assistance (odds ratio [OR], 3.71; P<0.001). In randomized Phase 4, AI assistance improved accuracy vs reference-sheet support alone (OR, 4.28; 95% CI, 3.08-5.95; P<0.001), and Grad-CAM provided additional benefit (OR, 1.53; 95% CI, 1.04-2.25; P=0.033). Exploratory analyses showed greater improvement among less experienced readers; with AI assistance, non-cardiologists outperformed cardiologists. AI-assisted readers remained less accurate overall than the model alone. ConclusionsAn ECG image-based ensemble differentiated Takotsubo syndrome from anterior STEMI and improved reader accuracy. Visual explanations provided additional benefit, while experience-related differences highlight the importance of effective human-AI interaction. Clinical PerspectiveO_ST_ABSWhat is new?C_ST_ABSO_LIAn electrocardiogram (ECG) image-based ensemble deep learning model differentiated Takotsubo syndrome from acute anterior ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction with an external-validation accuracy of 0.914 and ROC AUC of 0.970 and exceeded mean reader accuracy on the reader-study ECG sets. C_LIO_LIIn a human diagnostic test, displaying the models prediction improved readers diagnostic performance, and adding gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM) explanation produced further gains. C_LIO_LIExploratory analyses showed greater improvement and higher AI-assisted accuracy among less experienced readers, with reversal of cardiologists unaided advantage under AI assistance, motivating a utilization bias hypothesis. C_LI What Are the Clinical Implications?O_LIThe model exceeded mean unaided and AI-assisted reader accuracy on the reader-study ECG sets, supporting its potential to aid differentiation of Takotsubo syndrome from acute anterior myocardial infarction. C_LIO_LIAI assistance improved reader diagnostic accuracy, with further benefit from Grad-CAM visualizations, supporting further evaluation of these tools in clinical practice. C_LIO_LIConventional clinical expertise may not ensure effective AI use, warranting further studies to test the utilization bias hypothesis and determine whether training in integrating AI predictions can improve performance across reader backgrounds and experience levels. C_LI

infographic.key_insight: AI assistance improved readers’ ECG differentiation of Takotsubo syndrome from anterior STEMI, with a modest additional benefit from Grad-CAM heatmaps.
infographic.clinical_relevance: ECG-based AI could support this diagnostic distinction, but the study does not establish safety or benefit in real-time emergency care.
method: Developed a three-model deep learning ensemble using 12-lead ECG images from two hospitals.
Used self-supervised pretraining, fine-tuning, and external validation.
Studied 70 healthcare providers across four phases, including randomized comparison of reference sheets, AI predictions, and AI plus heatmaps.
infographic.evidence_signal: External-validation accuracy was 91.4% for Takotsubo–STEMI discrimination; estimated reader correctness rose from 63.2% unaided to 86.4% with AI assistance.

title: Longitudinal AI Models Predict Cancer Adverse Events
authors: Fu, C.; Yu, J.; Shi, R.; Waters, M.; Pavlak, M.; Arfe, A.; Shah, S. P.; Battle, A.; kehl, K. L.; Bot, B. M.; US Cancer AI Alliance, ; Schultz, N.; Morris, Q. D.; Jee, J.
abstract: Clinical interventions for cancer treatment toxicities can reduce morbidity, mortality, and healthcare cost, if high risk patients can be identified. We developed SPARC, a transformer-based foundation model, using real-world, longitudinal, routinely collected health measurements, to predict adverse event risk. Pre-training and fine-tuning SPARC on 101,920,379 measurements from 224,047 patients with cancer led to state-of-the-art performance at predicting cancer-related adverse events on (i) held-out data from the development cohort, (ii) a prospective validation cohort from the same center (Npatients=23,126), (iii) multiple publicly available external datasets (Npatients=26,012), and (iv) external, multi-hospital cohorts (Npatients=562,620, 206,840). SPARC generalized to multiple external centers and identified patients most likely to benefit from an intervention (G-CSF). Pooled multi-institution, more than single-institution, fine-tuning improved generalizability. We release SPARC as a community resource. Our results highlight the utility of AI time series models in oncologic management.

infographic.key_insight: SPARC, a transformer-based model of longitudinal health measurements, predicted cancer-related adverse events and generalized across multiple external centers.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Risk predictions could help target supportive care, with the study reporting identification of patients most likely to benefit from G-CSF.
method: Pre-trained and fine-tuned on routinely collected, longitudinal health measurements.
Evaluated on held-out, prospective same-center, and external cohorts.
Compared pooled multi-institution with single-institution fine-tuning.
infographic.evidence_signal: Training used 101,920,379 measurements from 224,047 patients; evaluation included a prospective cohort of 23,126 patients and external cohorts of 26,012, 562,620, and 206,840 patients.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish whether model-guided care improves patient outcomes; prospective clinical-impact evaluation remains needed.
infographic.paper_title: Longitudinal AI Models Predict Cancer Adverse Events

title: Coach-BP: Computer Vision-Based Assessment and Correction of Blood Pressure Measurement Technique
authors: Biswas, R.; Abad, A. J.; Nugas, J.; Shim, J.; Pletcher, M. J.; Lamprea-Montealegre, J. A.; Abbasi-Asl, R.
abstract: BackgroundAccurate blood pressure (BP) measurement, essential for hypertension care, requires proper technique. Posture errors can raise systolic BP by more than 20 mm Hg, yet technique is rarely verified objectively. We aimed to develop and evaluate Coach-BP, a computer vision system that detects technique errors from video to support real-time coaching. MethodsWe enrolled adults attending an academic cardiovascular prevention center between February and April 2026 and filmed BP measurements with front and side cameras. We analyzed 408 encounters from 225 participants. Coach-BP uses machine learning models trained on clinician labels to assess five American Heart Association criteria using pose, visual context, and audio-visual features. We evaluated its accuracy against expert clinician ratings by leave-one-participant-out cross-validation. We then examined robustness to simulated camera artifacts and interpreted the features important for each criterion. FindingsAt baseline, 138 (62%) of 223 participants had at least one technique error and 54 (24%) two or more. Coach-BP achieved a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0{middle dot}93 (95% CI 0{middle dot}90-0{middle dot}94), with 0{middle dot}97 (0{middle dot}94-0{middle dot}99) for legs uncrossed, 0{middle dot}97 (0{middle dot}93-1{middle dot}00) for no talking, 0{middle dot}92 (0{middle dot}85-0{middle dot}98) for back supported, 0{middle dot}91 (0{middle dot}86-0{middle dot}95) for feet flat, and 0{middle dot}86 (0{middle dot}81-0{middle dot}91) for arm supported at heart level. Mean balanced accuracy was 0{middle dot}88 (0{middle dot}85-0{middle dot}90). Performance was robust to simulated camera shift, zoom, and rotation. Its models relied on features clinicians would assess, such as cuffed-hand height and foot position. One model classified back support similarly from either camera. InterpretationCoach-BP accurately detected errors in the five guideline-recommended criteria of BP measurement technique from clinic video, enabling objective assessment of each criterion. FundingUniversity of California San Francisco Cardiology Scholars Award. Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSWe searched PubMed and Europe PMC from database inception to Oct 10, 2026, without language restriction, for studies in adults that automatically assessed any guideline-recommended patient condition during seated upper-arm blood pressure measurement, using terms including "blood pressure", "measurement technique", "posture", "computer vision", "pose estimation", and "sensor". A systematic review of 328 studies and a randomized crossover trial of arm position have quantified the effect of individual errors, several of which raise systolic blood pressure by 5 mm Hg or more, and studies that observed or filmed patients measuring their blood pressure found errors in almost all patients. Three studies assessed measurement conditions automatically, all with the same sensor-equipped chair, which recorded rest time, back support, crossed legs, and ambient noise during self-measurement. They were small (41-113 participants), and only one compared the chairs output with direct observation. In one, adherence was high only for the conditions on which the chair gave live guidance. None used video, and the chair did not assess arm or foot position. The evidence on the effect of errors includes a randomized trial, whereas the evidence on automated assessment is limited to these small observational studies of one device. Added value of this studyIn 225 adults contributing 408 blood pressure measurement encounters, technique errors were present at the first reading in 138 (62%) of 223 participants and did not differ significantly across the self-reported characteristics examined, including home blood pressure monitoring. Among 171 participants re-measured after staff-delivered coaching, the number with any technique error fell from 128 (75%) to 12 (7%). Coach-BP assessed all five guideline-recommended posture and behavior criteria directly from clinic video, with a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0{middle dot}93 under leave-one-participant-out cross-validation. Coach-BP matched or improved on rule-based baselines for all five criteria, with gains for feet flat, the arm criterion, back supported, and no talking. Performance remained stable when the image was shifted, rescaled, or rotated, suggesting robustness to differences in how the camera frames the patient. One back-support model performed similarly from the side and front cameras, so a single front camera placed as in the study could assess all five criteria. Implications of all the available evidenceTechnique errors were common, including among patients who already monitor blood pressure at home, and most were corrected after brief staff coaching. Coach-BP shows that five criteria of blood pressure measurement technique can be assessed automatically and accurately from ordinary video. Together, these findings support automated feedback at the time of measurement as a scalable way to improve technique, particularly at home, where no one checks it. Prospective studies should now test this in home settings and more diverse populations.

infographic.key_insight: Coach-BP detected five blood pressure measurement technique criteria from clinic video with a mean AUROC of 0.93.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Automated technique assessment could support more consistent blood pressure measurement, but effects on blood pressure accuracy and patient outcomes were not reported.
method: Analyzed front- and side-camera recordings using pose, visual context, and audio-visual features.
Trained machine learning models on clinician labels for five guideline-recommended technique criteria.
Evaluated against expert ratings using leave-one-participant-out cross-validation and simulated camera artifacts.
infographic.evidence_signal: In 408 encounters from 225 participants at one academic center, mean AUROC was 0.93 (95% CI 0.90–0.94) and mean balanced accuracy was 0.88 (0.85–0.90).
infographic.watch_item: Single-center cross-validation does not establish performance in other settings or the effectiveness of real-time corrective coaching.
infographic.paper_title: Coach-BP: Computer Vision-Based Assessment and Correction of Blood Pressure Measurement Technique

title: PedDx: An End-to-End Deep Learning Framework for Pediatric Posterior Fossa Tumor Diagnosis with Agentic AI-Enabled Independent External Evaluation
authors: Fathi Kazerooni, A.; Batal, F.; Vunnava, B.; Damaraju, E.; Tavallaii, A.; Gandhi, D.; Gottipati, A.; Zhu, P.; Chrysochoou, D.; Varshochi, S.; Adib Moradi, S.; Familiar, A. M.; Chiang, A.; Vaghani, Y.; Azemi, G.; Doig, M.; To, M.-S.; Luck, A.; Kim, M. C.; Khalili, N.; Khalili, N.; Jain, P.; Lee, C.; Hansford, J. R.; Di Ieva, A.; Storm, P. B.; Resnick, A. C.; Reddy, K.; Vossough, A.; Nabavizadeh, A.
abstract: Reliable clinical translation of diagnostic artificial intelligence (AI) requires evaluation beyond classification accuracy. We developed PedDx, a segmentation-free framework for pediatric posterior fossa tumor diagnosis using T2-weighted MRI, pretrained 3DINO representations, calibrated predictions, and confidence-based abstention. Evaluation included 492 discovery, 114 replication, 129 external validation, and 40 independently tested cases, alongside 236 out-of-distribution (OOD) cases and controlled imaging perturbations. Classification accuracy was 79.8% in replication and 81.4% in external validation, increasing to 90.5% and 88.7%, respectively, among non-abstained cases. OOD analyses revealed performance degradation and confidently incorrect predictions, while perturbation analyses identified acquisition and alignment vulnerabilities. An external institution independently executed the complete agentic workflow, successfully generating predictions and structured quality-control reports for all 40 cases, with classification accuracy of 92.5%, increasing to 97.3% among non-abstained cases. PedDx demonstrates how uncertainty assessment, failure-mode characterization, external validation, and independently reproducible, traceable reporting can collectively inform the reliability and limitations of diagnostic AI systems.

infographic.key_insight: PedDx classified pediatric posterior fossa tumors from T2-weighted MRI, with higher accuracy among cases retained after confidence-based abstention.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The framework could support diagnostic assessment, but confident errors and imaging vulnerabilities limit readiness for routine clinical use.
method: Segmentation-free classification using pretrained 3DINO representations.
Calibrated predictions with confidence-based abstention.
Agentic workflow for independently generated predictions and structured quality-control reports.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation included 492 discovery, 114 replication, 129 external validation, 40 independently tested, and 236 out-of-distribution cases; accuracy rose from 79.8% to 90.5% in replication, 81.4% to 88.7% in external validation, and 92.5% to 97.3% in independent testing when restricted to non-abstained cases.
infographic.watch_item: Out-of-distribution cases produced confidently incorrect predictions, and imaging perturbations exposed acquisition and alignment vulnerabilities; higher non-abstained accuracy does not represent all-case performance.
infographic.paper_title: PedDx: An End-to-End Deep Learning Framework for Pediatric Posterior Fossa Tumor Diagnosis with Agentic AI-Enabled Independent External Evaluation

title: Genetic hallmarks of patients with congenital portosystemic shunts and portopulmonary hypertension: protocol for a multicentre exploratory study
authors: Schepens, I.; van Steenbeek, F.; Pont, F.; Wacker, J.; Joye, R.; Beghetti, M.; Makrythanasis, P.; McLin, V. A.
abstract: IntroductionCongenital portosystemic shunts (CPSS) are rare vascular malformations, with an estimated prevalence of 1/30000 live births, that cause portal blood to partly bypass the liver. CPSS frequently co-occur with congenital heart disease and other malformations, suggesting a shared developmental or genetic basis. Severe acquired clinical manifestations are present in a large proportion of patients with CPSS. Portopulmonary hypertension (PoPH), the most life-threatening, has been reported in as many as 7-14% of CPSS patients. Mounting evidence indicates that PoPH can arise early in life, particularly in children with CPSS, yet paediatric PoPH remains understudied. This project aims to identify genetic variants associated with PoPH in CPSS patients through whole-genomes, focusing primarily on known pathogenic genes for pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), congenital heart disease (CHD), Hereditary Haemorrhagic Telangiectasia (HHT), SNPs previously associated with PoPH in adults, and ultimately novel genomic variants. The overarching goal of the study is to improve personalised risk assessment and inform clinical decisions regarding elective shunt closure in individuals potentially at-risk of developing PoPH. Methods and analysisThe aim is to perform an international multi-centre exploratory genome analysis of patients with CPSS and PoPH identified through the International Registry of Congenital Portosystemic Shunts (IRCPSS). Whole-genome sequencing will be utilized to analyse both coding and non-coding regions in a predominantly paediatric cohort. Targeted analysis of established pathogenic genes associated with PAH, CHD, HHT, and PoPH will be complemented by a genome-wide approach to identify novel, potentially pathogenic variants, with variant classification assessed according to American College of Medical Genetics (ACMG) criteria. Family-based analyses, including trio analyses and segregation studies, will enable the identification of dominant, recessive, and de novo variants, facilitating a comprehensive evaluation of variant inheritance pattern and pathogenic potential. Ethics and disseminationThis study has been approved by the CCER (Geneva cantonal ethics committee for research) and poses minimal risk to participants, limited to blood sampling performed as part of routine clinical care for patients. Genetic data will be securely stored and analysed in compliance with GDPR. Clinically significant findings will be communicated through recruiting physicians, in accordance with participant preference regarding incidental findings. Study results will be disseminated through open-access peer-reviewed publications and scientific conferences to advance understanding and management of PoPH in individuals with CPSS and potentially other chronic liver diseases associated with portosystemic bypass. ClinicalTrials.govNCT07314814 CCER Ethical approval2024-01698 STRENGTHS AND LIMITATIONS OF THIS STUDYO_LISystematic analysis of established gene panels for PAH, CHD and HHT, to diagnose referenced genetic disorders. C_LIO_LIThe trio-based whole-genome analysis design allows for the detection of novel potentially pathogenic variants and genes. C_LIO_LIThe rarity of CPSS limits recruitment to an expected sample size of ~30 trios, both a realistic target for a rare disease study and appropriate family-based analyses. C_LIO_LILeverages the International Registry of Congenital Portosystemic Shunts as a resource for correlating genetic and clinical data C_LI

infographic.key_insight: This study protocol will explore genetic variants linked to portopulmonary hypertension (PoPH) in patients with congenital portosystemic shunts (CPSS).
infographic.clinical_relevance: Findings could eventually improve PoPH risk assessment and inform elective shunt-closure decisions, but clinical utility is not yet established.
method: International, multicentre recruitment through the International Registry of Congenital Portosystemic Shunts.
Whole-genome sequencing with targeted and genome-wide searches for potentially pathogenic variants.
ACMG variant classification plus trio and family segregation analyses to assess inheritance.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes a planned, predominantly paediatric genomic study; it reports no sample size, genetic findings or predictive performance.
infographic.watch_item: This is an exploratory genomics protocol, not an AI evaluation; any discovered associations will require validation before clinical use.
infographic.paper_title: Genetic hallmarks of patients with congenital portosystemic shunts and portopulmonary hypertension: protocol for a multicentre exploratory study

title: Evaluating ChatGPTs Responses to Chiropractic Patient Questions: A Comparative Study
authors: Pham, A. V.; Peterson, A. C.; Tom, J. C.; Jones, A. L.; Daniels, C. J.
abstract: BackgroundLarge language models (LLMs) are used at an increased frequency by patients to answer health related questions. Prior studies have evaluated LLMs and their performance with musculoskeletal (MSK) and spine domains, but have not been used to evaluate chiropractic-relevant content. ObjectiveTo evaluate ChatGPT responses to commonly asked chiropractic patient questions for concordance with chiropractic clinical practice guidelines. MethodsThirty questions addressing low back pain, neck pain, and chronic musculoskeletal pain were developed based on current U.S. chiropractic clinical practice guidelines (CPGs). ChatGPT (GPT-5.2) generated responses in isolated sessions. Responses were assessed for readability using established indices, then five licensed chiropractors independently rated each response using a 5-point Likert scale across four domains: relevance, clarity, completeness, and accuracy. Inter-rater reliability was evaluated using Krippendorffs alpha (ordinal). ResultsReadability measures demonstrated that ChatGPT responses were written at approximately a college-level reading grade. Expert ratings across all domain means (standard deviation) were predominately clustered at the upper end of rating scale (1-5): Relevance 4.72 {+/-} 0.56; Clarity 4.76 {+/-} 0.50; Completeness 4.23 {+/-} 0.81; Accuracy 4.00 {+/-} 1.02. The Krippendorffs alpha (ordinal) ranged from -0.023-0.214 across the domains, all reflective of poor inter-rater reliability. ConclusionChatGPT responses were broadly consistent with chiropractic CPGs, though readability levels exceeded recommended patient education standards. While the expert panel frequently assigned similar scores, minor scoring differences and restricted score distributions produced low chance-corrected reliability. These findings suggest that ChatGPT can produce guideline concordant responses but readability and interpretive variability should be considered when integrating LLM generated information into patient education.

infographic.key_insight: ChatGPT responses were broadly consistent with chiropractic guidelines, but college-level readability and poor rater agreement temper the findings.
infographic.clinical_relevance: LLM-generated chiropractic education may need simpler language and clinician review before patient-facing use.
method: Developed 30 questions on low back, neck, and chronic musculoskeletal pain using U.S. chiropractic guidelines.
Generated GPT-5.2 responses in isolated sessions and assessed readability.
Five licensed chiropractors independently rated relevance, clarity, completeness, and accuracy on 5-point scales.
infographic.evidence_signal: Mean ratings ranged from 4.00/5 for accuracy to 4.76/5 for clarity, while ordinal Krippendorff’s alpha ranged from −0.023 to 0.214, indicating poor inter-rater reliability.
infographic.watch_item: High average ratings do not establish dependable clinical accuracy, particularly given poor rater agreement and evaluation of only 30 questions.
infographic.paper_title: Evaluating ChatGPTs Responses to Chiropractic Patient Questions: A Comparative Study

title: Biopsy-Validated Deep Learning Mapping of Glioma Infiltration Beyond Contrast Enhancement Using Multiparametric MRI
authors: Wujek, R. T.; Schmainda, K. M.; Prah, M. A.
abstract: BackgroundGlioblastoma (GBM) exhibits diffuse tumor infiltration beyond contrast-enhancing margins into FLAIR-hyperintense brain tissue, where infiltrative tumor is not visible on conventional MRI. We developed and validated the infiltrative Tumor Burden (iTB) map, a deep learning biomarker that uses multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) to identify infiltrative tumor within these non-enhancing regions. MethodsPreoperative mpMRI datasets from 80 patients with WHO grade II-IV gliomas and 24 patients with brain metastases were retrospectively analyzed. Imaging included pre- and post-contrast T1-weighted, T2-weighted, FLAIR, dynamic susceptibility contrast perfusion and diffusion MRI-derived maps (rCBV, rCBF, ADC). Spatially localized stereotactic biopsies from non-enhancing glioma regions provided histopathologic ground truth while peritumoral brain metastasis regions served as biologically grounded non-tumor controls. A 3D convolutional neural network was trained on voxel-centered mpMRI patches using patient-level cross-validation and an independent test set, with data augmentation optimized using a greedy local search strategy. ResultsModel development included 121 biopsy-localized samples from 56 glioma patients and 104 non-tumor samples from 26 brain metastasis patients. Augmentation optimization significantly improved independent test-set performance, increasing accuracy from 74.5% to 85.5% and AUC from 0.859 to 0.942 (p = 0.008). Ensemble-derived voxel-wise iTB maps demonstrated low infiltration probabilities in brain metastases and extensive regions of elevated infiltration probability in glioblastoma, consistent with expected biology. ConclusionsThe iTB biomarker generates voxel-wise maps of tumor infiltration within non-enhancing FLAIR abnormalities. Validated against image-localized histopathology and independent testing, it achieved high diagnostic performance and may improve surgical planning, radiotherapy targeting, and assessment of glioma burden.

infographic.key_insight: A deep learning MRI biomarker mapped glioma infiltration beyond contrast-enhancing margins, achieving an independent-test AUC of 0.942.
infographic.clinical_relevance: These infiltration maps could help inform surgical planning, radiotherapy targeting, and glioma burden assessment, but clinical benefit remains unproven.
method: Trained a 3D convolutional neural network on multiparametric MRI patches.
Used localized glioma biopsies as ground truth and peritumoral metastasis tissue as non-tumor controls.
Applied patient-level cross-validation, independent testing, and optimized data augmentation.
infographic.evidence_signal: In this retrospective study, augmentation optimization increased independent-test accuracy from 74.5% to 85.5% and AUC from 0.859 to 0.942 (reported p = 0.008).
infographic.watch_item: Prospective validation across institutions is needed before using these maps to guide treatment.
infographic.paper_title: Biopsy-Validated Deep Learning Mapping of Glioma Infiltration Beyond Contrast Enhancement Using Multiparametric MRI

title: Same pipelines, different answers: how evaluation design shapes EEG seizure prediction
authors: song, z.; Pedersen, M.; Henare, D.
abstract: Seizure-prediction studies on scalp electroencephalography (EEG) often report accuracies that would be clinically useful, yet the score a model receives also depends on how its test data were separated from its training data. We kept five published pipelines fixed, from a spectral baseline (power spectral density with linear discriminant analysis, PSD+LDA) to a transformer, and changed only how they were evaluated on the CHB-MIT database. When whole subjects were held out in 20 repeated partitions, every pipeline scored close to the 0.5 reference (mean area under the ROC curve, AUC, 0.527-0.553), and the five pipelines differed less from one another than each varied between partitions. Within patients, PSD+LDA reached an AUC of 0.815 when windows were allocated at random but 0.572 when each preictal block was kept intact and later seizures were held out for testing. Tracing every window back to its recording showed that an index-based within-patient split had let raw EEG samples cross the train-test boundary in all ten eligible cases. Thresholds tuned to allow 1.67% false positives on validation data did not hold that rate on new subjects, and at those thresholds only 2-6% of preictal windows were detected. A zero-shot test of the baseline on the Siena database gave an AUC of 0.480. In this benchmark, the choice of evaluation changed the answer far more than the choice of architecture. We release the window manifests, partitions and predictions so that new models can be tested on the same terms. All results concern retrospective window classification, not continuous alarms.

infographic.key_insight: How EEG seizure-prediction models were evaluated changed their scores far more than which of five architectures was used.
infographic.clinical_relevance: High retrospective scores may not translate to reliable seizure prediction for new patients or future seizures.
method: Kept five published pipelines fixed, from PSD+LDA to a transformer, on CHB-MIT EEG data.
Compared subject-held-out testing with random-window and chronological, intact-preictal-block splits within patients.
Traced windows for train–test overlap and tested the baseline without adaptation on Siena data.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 20 subject-held-out partitions, mean AUCs were 0.527–0.553; within-patient PSD+LDA fell from 0.815 with random windows to 0.572 with chronological, intact-block testing.
infographic.watch_item: These results concern retrospective window classification, not continuous seizure alarms or demonstrated clinical utility.
infographic.paper_title: Same pipelines, different answers: how evaluation design shapes EEG seizure prediction

title: Multiscale Spatial Characterization of Glioma MRI with MUSE and Radiomics
authors: Miola, M.; Cammarasana, S.
abstract: PurposeCharacterizing glioma heterogeneity requires measurements that retain the physical scale and orientation of intratumoral intensity dependence. We evaluate the original 3D variographic field produced by the MUSE tool (Modeling Uncertainty as a Support for the Environment) alongside directional radiomics and independent image-based molecular classification. MethodsWe analyzed postcontrast T1-weighted magnetic resonance images and enhancing-tumor segmentations from the public UCSF-PDGM collection. Verified MUSE outputs were available for 416 independent baseline patients, of whom 375 had paired directional gray-level co-occurrence matrix (GLCM) measurements. Each MUSE field retained 328 original experimental directional variograms with physical lag distances, semivariances, orientations, and voxel-pair support. Agreement was assessed at aligned offsets and through between-tumor comparisons. Patient-level permutation tests evaluated associations with isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) status on 2,508 native direction-lag coordinates. A standalone 3D residual convolutional neural network (CNN) provided a separate IDH classification benchmark. ResultsAt 9,371 geometrically aligned offsets, native MUSE semivariance and half GLCM contrast correlated strongly (Pearson r = 0.954). Across 31,599 eligible between-tumor comparisons, representation-level dissimilarities showed Spearman{rho} S = 0.862, with sensitivity to GLCM feature family and long-offset sampling support. In 364 grade-4 tumors, including 24 IDH-mutant cases, the original MUSE field was associated with IDH after conventional adjustment (global permutation p = 0.00050), but the association was attenuated after primary directional GLCM adjustment (p = 0.256). The independent CNN achieved an out-of-fold IDH ROC-AUC of 0.792 and PR-AUC of 0.414 across 416 patients. Native MUSE examples revealed scale- and direction-dependent spatial behavior, including distances beyond those sampled by the GLCM protocol. ConclusionVariograms by MUSE provide a physically indexed description of tumor spatial heterogeneity that can accompany radiomic analysis and CNN classification. The observed statistical overlap is substantial, and incremental clinical discrimination beyond directional GLCM features remains unestablished.

infographic.key_insight: MUSE variograms describe glioma MRI heterogeneity by physical distance and direction, with substantial overlap with directional radiomics.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This research approach may complement tumor imaging analysis, but it does not establish clinical utility for IDH prediction or treatment decisions.
method: Analyzed postcontrast T1-weighted MRI and enhancing-tumor segmentations from 416 UCSF-PDGM patients.
Compared native 3D MUSE variograms with directional GLCM radiomics in 375 paired cases.
Tested IDH associations using patient-level permutations and evaluated a separate 3D CNN classifier.
infographic.evidence_signal: MUSE and half GLCM contrast correlated strongly across 9,371 aligned offsets (r = 0.954); the separate CNN achieved out-of-fold IDH ROC-AUC 0.792 and PR-AUC 0.414.
infographic.watch_item: In 364 grade-4 tumors, only 24 were IDH-mutant, and the MUSE–IDH association weakened after directional GLCM adjustment (p = 0.256), limiting evidence of added molecular information.
infographic.paper_title: Multiscale Spatial Characterization of Glioma MRI with MUSE and Radiomics

title: SPEECH FEATURES IN A DEVELOPMENTAL PERSPECTIVE: A SCREENING TOOL FOR PSYCHOSIS, DEPRESSION AND ANXIETY
authors: Ribeiro, M.; Amorim, J.; Malcorra, B.; Piccolo, R.; Jensen, L.; Soares, D.; Meletti, T.; Mota, N. B.
abstract: Language production provides a window into cognitive development, social cognition, and mental health. To translate this potential into clinical practice, we developed a scalable speech-based platform integrating graph-theoretical, psycholinguistic, and emotional features from brief spontaneous narratives to support developmental monitoring, mental wellness screening, and clinical decision-making. Normative developmental trajectories were derived from 2149 participants spanning 0-23 years of formal education. Narratives elicited using positively valenced pictures were transformed into word graphs to derive two composite indices: Narrative Complexity (NC), reflecting structural language organization, and Emotional Narrative Complexity (ENC), integrating narrative structure and emotional content. Both indices were modeled using asymptotic functions calibrated by schooling and converted into percentile-based normative curves. NC (R{superscript 2} = 0.29, {tau} = 7.77) and ENC (R{superscript 2} = 0.31, {tau} = 6.97) increased with schooling, approaching saturation around middle school. These trajectories provide educationally calibrated references for evaluating linguistic and socioemotional development. Clinical utility was investigated in a transdiagnostic sample of 120 participants, comprising healthy controls (n = 38), mood disorders (n = 28), affective psychosis (n = 36), and non-affective psychosis (n = 18). Although ENC alone did not discriminate between symptom-risk or diagnostic groups, classifiers combining its constituent variables with education and sex achieved AUCs of 0.726 for symptom risk and 0.800 for diagnosis, increasing to 0.774 and 0.858, respectively, with additional linguistic features. Machine-learning models integrating graph-derived, psycholinguistic, and emotional features further estimated symptom dimensions assessed by PANSS, GAD-7, and PHQ-9, achieving AUCs of 0.74-0.92 across severity thresholds while maintaining sensitivity [≥] 0.80. Individual linguistic variables also differed significantly across symptom-severity strata, suggesting distinct associations with psychopathological dimensions. Together, these findings establish an integrated speech-based framework spanning normative developmental assessment, mental wellness screening, and symptom-informed clinical support. By combining educationally calibrated trajectories with interpretable linguistic features and machine learning, this approach offers scalable digital markers to identify atypical developmental patterns, inform preventive strategies, and assist clinical assessment and decision-making.

infographic.key_insight: Brief speech narratives combined with linguistic AI features showed potential for education-calibrated developmental monitoring and mental health screening.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Speech-based models may support assessment of psychosis, depression, and anxiety symptoms, but these findings do not establish a standalone diagnostic tool.
method: Derived narrative complexity and emotional narrative complexity indices from picture-elicited speech.
Built schooling-calibrated normative curves using 2,149 participants.
Combined graph-derived, psycholinguistic, and emotional features in machine-learning models.
infographic.evidence_signal: In a 120-person transdiagnostic sample, expanded classifiers achieved AUCs of 0.774 for symptom risk and 0.858 for diagnosis; symptom-severity models reported AUCs of 0.74–0.92 with sensitivity ≥0.80.
infographic.watch_item: Emotional narrative complexity alone did not distinguish groups, and the abstract does not report external validation of the models.
infographic.paper_title: SPEECH FEATURES IN A DEVELOPMENTAL PERSPECTIVE: A SCREENING TOOL FOR PSYCHOSIS, DEPRESSION AND ANXIETY

title: Large language models detect methodological errors that human peer review misses in clinical trials
authors: Brian, D.; Pereira Hernandez, X. I.; Yin, H.; Koury, J.; Rust, R.
abstract: Peer review is the principal quality control of published research, but methodological errors can go undetected. In an earlier experiment with errors inserted into three reports of randomized clinical trials, untrained human reviewers achieved a mean major-error detection score of 27%. Here, we tested whether 15 large language models (LLMs), including four open-weight models, detect the same errors. Their major-error detection scores ranged from 53% to 96%. To reduce the risk of memorization, we repeated the test on three clinical trials published in 2026. Scores ranged from 51% to 99%, and from 66% to 87% for the open-weight models. Notably, LLMs still flagged 2% to 29% of the error types in control reports without inserted errors, most often conclusions not supported by the results and missing reasons why screened patients were not enrolled. Across the 12 models, mean review times ranged from 1.4 to 16.3 minutes. Opus 5.5 achieved the highest major-error detection score (99%), while GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Luna offered cost-effective alternatives with scores of 92% and 87%, respectively. Together, these tests provide a benchmark for specialized review models and suggest that relying on human peer review alone may leave avoidable methodological errors undetected.

infographic.key_insight: In tests using clinical trial reports with inserted methodological errors, LLMs detected more major errors than untrained human reviewers had in an earlier experiment.
infographic.clinical_relevance: LLM-assisted review could help identify methodological problems in clinical research, but false alarms require expert verification.
method: Tested 15 LLMs, including four open-weight models, on three trial reports with inserted errors.
Repeated testing on three trials published in 2026 to reduce memorization risk.
Evaluated control reports without inserted errors and measured review times.
infographic.evidence_signal: Major-error detection scores ranged from 53%–96% in the initial test and 51%–99% in the repeat test, versus 27% for untrained human reviewers in the earlier experiment.
infographic.watch_item: Models also flagged 2%–29% of error types in control reports, and performance on a small, deliberately altered report set may not generalize to routine peer review.
infographic.paper_title: Large language models detect methodological errors that human peer review misses in clinical trials

title: EM-BENCH: A Reproducible Framework for Benchmarking Guideline-Concordant Clinical Decision Making in Large Language Models
authors: Nguyen, N.; Perice, L.; Sangal, R.; Kumar, V.; Chu, A.; Dash, D.
abstract: BackgroundPhysicians increasingly use artificial intelligence tools to support clinical work, yet there is no accepted standard for measuring the competency of large language models (LLMs) in clinical decision support. We developed EM-BENCH, a physician-validated, deterministically scored benchmark for evaluating whether models reliably apply the American College of Emergency Physicians (ACEP) guidelines to clinical decisions. MethodsEM-BENCH comprises 210 binary clinical vignettes covering all 70 critical questions across 25 ACEP clinical policies. We evaluated 149 LLM configurations representing 79 base models using prespecified answers and deterministic scoring. Each vignette had a prespecified correct answer to a binary yes-or-no question based on an ACEP recommendation. We examined associations between accuracy and model access tier (closed-access vs. open-weight models), model size, release date, clinical policy, recommendation evidence level, and reasoning settings. ResultsNo configuration achieved complete guideline concordance. The highest performing configuration answered 207 of 210 vignettes correctly (98.6%). Closed-access models outperformed open-weight models (median accuracy, 91% vs. 63%; Hodges-Lehmann location shift, 26 percentage points; 99% CI, 20 to 33; adjusted P<0.001). Among open-weight model families, a 10-fold increase in parameter count was associated with a 14-percentage-point increase in accuracy (99% CI, 7.7 to 20; adjusted P<0.001). Across all models, accuracy increased by 8.9 percentage points per release year (99% CI, 3.6 to 14; adjusted P<0.001). Neither enabling a thinking mode (pseudomedian change, 0.95 percentage points; 99% CI, -2.6 to 3.1; adjusted P=1.00) nor high versus low reasoning effort (0.91 percentage points; 99% CI, -0.69 to 3.1; adjusted P=0.56) consistently improved accuracy. ConclusionsContemporary LLMs showed improving but incomplete ability to apply ACEP guidelines. Concordance varied markedly across models and was associated with access tier, size, and release recency, while additional inference-time reasoning offered inconsistent benefit. Specialty-specific, physician-validated benchmarks may provide a reproducible assessment of LLMs ability to make guideline-concordant clinical decisions.

infographic.key_insight: LLMs showed improving but incomplete ACEP guideline concordance, with the best configuration scoring 98.6% and no consistent benefit from added reasoning.
infographic.clinical_relevance: EM-BENCH offers a reproducible way to assess guideline application in emergency medicine, without establishing safety or effectiveness in patient care.
method: 210 physician-validated, binary vignettes spanning 70 critical questions across 25 ACEP clinical policies.
149 configurations representing 79 base models evaluated using prespecified answers and deterministic scoring.
Accuracy compared by access tier, model size, release date, policy, evidence level, and reasoning settings.
infographic.evidence_signal: The top configuration answered 207/210 correctly; median accuracy was 91% for closed-access versus 63% for open-weight models.
infographic.watch_item: Performance on binary guideline vignettes may not generalize to complex clinical workflows or patient outcomes.
infographic.paper_title: EM-BENCH: A Reproducible Framework for Benchmarking Guideline-Concordant Clinical Decision Making in Large Language Models

title: An Agentic AI Pipeline for an Evidence-Grounded Environmental Health Public Information System: Development and Evaluation
authors: Ingebretsen, S. H.; Gouripeddi, R.; Facelli, J.; Cummins, M.; Shah-mohammadi, F.
abstract: BackgroundExisting environmental and health information systems typically provide isolated data streams, requiring users to interpret heterogeneous information sources without personalized guidance. Residents and health providers of urban regions with complex environmental conditions, such as the Salt Lake Valley, frequently seek timely, location-specific information about weather, air quality, and their associated health impacts, but may find it difficult to integrate this information in their decision-making, precluding the effective translation of valuable environmental health information into action. ObjectiveThis study aimed to develop and evaluate an agentic artificial intelligence (AI) pipeline that delivers evidence-grounded, neighborhood-scale responses to health-related environmental questions raised lay persons by dynamically orchestrating authoritative weather, neighborhood-scale environmental observations, air quality, and health-evidence resources. MethodsWe developed an agentic AI pipeline using LangGraph and OpenAI large language models to interpret natural language queries, select and invoke relevant external tools, retrieve real-time environmental data and evidence-based health guidance, and synthesize responses. The pipeline integrates multiple authoritative resources, including weather forecasts, air-quality observations, geospatial services, and a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) module built from asthma-related clinical guidance. The system incorporates fallback mechanisms to improve robustness when external services are unavailable. We evaluated the pipeline using a curated benchmark of representative user questions, assessing tool-needed recognition, correct tool selection, avoidance of irrelevant tools, parameter mapping, analytic pathway selection, and incorporation of tool outputs into the final response. ResultsThe developed system successfully integrated heterogeneous environmental and health information sources into a unified conversational interface that produces evidence-grounded, neighborhood-scale responses for the Salt Lake Valley. Evaluation demonstrated generally strong tool recognition, parameter mapping, and incorporation of retrieved information across diverse question types, supporting the pipelines ability to retrieve and integrate authoritative environmental and health information consumable by lay persons and providing an important step for the T3 and T4 phases of the translational pipeline of exposure health informatics. ConclusionsBy combining existing environmental health knowledge with local sensor observations and neighborhood-scale environmental measurements, and authoritative state and national weather and air quality resources, the system delivers more localized and context-aware guidance than approaches that rely on authoritative regional or state-level information. Rather than depending on the internal knowledge of a large language model, the pipeline dynamically retrieves, synthesizes, and attributes evidence from authoritative sources. The modular architecture enables seamless integration of additional environmental data streams, health knowledge sources, and geographic regions, providing a scalable foundation for future translational pipelines, completing the T3 to T4 path for environmental health.

infographic.key_insight: An agentic AI pipeline combines environmental data and health evidence to answer neighborhood-specific environmental health questions in the Salt Lake Valley.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The system could help residents and health providers contextualize local weather and air quality using asthma-related guidance, but clinical benefit was not established.
method: Used LangGraph and OpenAI models to interpret questions and orchestrate external tools.
Integrated weather, air-quality, geospatial, and neighborhood environmental data with retrieval of asthma-related clinical guidance.
Added fallback mechanisms for unavailable external services.
infographic.evidence_signal: A curated question benchmark assessed tool use, parameter mapping, analytic pathways, and response grounding; the partial abstract reports generally strong performance but provides no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Benchmark performance does not establish real-world reliability or improved health outcomes.
infographic.paper_title: An Agentic AI Pipeline for an Evidence-Grounded Environmental Health Public Information System: Development and Evaluation

title: Spatial AI quantification of inflammatory and architectural features differentiates pathologist-defined active ulcerative colitis from histological remission
authors: Windell, D.; Magness, A.; Li, R.; Davis, T.; Thomaides Brears, H.; Larkin, S.; Beyer, C.; Aljabar, P.; Kainth, R.; Wakefield, P.; Langford, C.; Powell, N.; DeLegge, M.; Bateman, A. C.; Feakins, R.; Fryer, E.; Goldin, R.; Landy, J.
abstract: Background and AimsArtificial intelligence (AI) is applied to histological assessment in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), but most approaches quantify features without considering anatomical location. We developed and evaluated PAIR-IBD (Perspectum AI Reading in IBD), an AI system quantifying inflammatory cell, crypt injury, and epithelial damage within mucosal compartments to distinguish histologically-defined active disease, remission, and inconclusive cases in ulcerative colitis (UC), in a single clinical network. MethodsA deep-learning ensemble was trained on three IBD datasets to identify lymphocytes, neutrophils, eosinophils, and plasma cells, and segment crypts, lamina propria (LP), surface epithelium and muscularis mucosae. Inflammatory cell densities and crypt injury metrics (mucin depletion, solidity, roughness, branching, and abscesses) were quantified. PAIR-IBD outputs were compared between pathologist-defined active UC and histological remission, evaluated in discordant cases and correlated with manual grading. ResultsCompared with Nancy remission, active biopsies showed 2.1-fold higher LP neutrophil, 5.3-fold higher crypt neutrophil and 1.2-fold higher LP lymphocyte density. Active UC showed increased mucin depletion, crypt branching, and crypt abscesses, with reduced crypt solidity (p<0.0001 for all). PAIR-IBD metrics correlated with manual pathology scores and global indices, strongest for mucin depletion, crypt neutrophils, crypt roughness and reduced crypt solidity (rs=0.50-0.73). Up to 89% of inconclusive biopsies aligned with histological remission-like profiles for individual metrics, particularly mucin depletion. ConclusionPAIR-IBD provides spatially resolved, quantitative assessment of inflammation, epithelial injury and crypt architecture in UC, with potential to support the characterization of inconclusive histology, complement scoring and contribute to histological endpoint assessment in clinical trials, pending validation. What is already known on this topicHistological remission is a key treatment target in ulcerative colitis (UC), but assessment relies on ordinal pathologist scoring systems (Nancy Index, Robarts Histopathological Index, Geboes Score) that are subject to inter-rater variability. What this study addsWe developed and evaluated PAIR-IBD, an artificial intelligence system quantifying inflammatory cell populations, crypt injury and epithelial damage across mucosal compartments in a single clinical network cohort. PAIR-IBD distinguished pathologist-defined active UC from remission and showed that inconclusive biopsies display a mixed rather than uniformly active or remission-like histological profile. How this study might affect research, practice or policyThese findings support further evaluation of PAIR-IBD as an adjunct to conventional histological scoring, with potential applications in clinical trial endpoint assessment and adjudication of discordant biopsies, pending external validation.

infographic.key_insight: PAIR-IBD quantified spatial inflammation and crypt architecture differences between pathologist-defined active ulcerative colitis and histological remission.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The system could complement pathology scoring and help characterize inconclusive biopsies, pending further validation.
method: Trained a deep-learning ensemble on three inflammatory bowel disease datasets.
Identified inflammatory cells and segmented mucosal compartments to quantify cell densities, crypt injury and epithelial damage.
Compared AI measurements with pathologist-defined disease activity and manual scores.
infographic.evidence_signal: In a single clinical network, active biopsies had 5.3-fold higher crypt neutrophil density than Nancy-defined remission, while selected AI metrics correlated with manual scores (Spearman rs=0.50–0.73).
infographic.watch_item: Single-network evaluation limits generalizability; independent validation is needed before clinical implementation.
infographic.paper_title: Spatial AI quantification of inflammatory and architectural features differentiates pathologist-defined active ulcerative colitis from histological remission

title: Tumor Associated Neutrophils Extend NETs To Spatially Drive Necroptosis In Glioblastoma
authors: Vaddi, P.; Zhuang, Y.; Liu, L.; Ingersoll, S.; Lee, S.; Gao, B.; van Bokhoven, A.; Harris, B. T.; Pine, S. R.; Sabaawy, H. E.
abstract: BackgroundGlioblastoma is pathologically characterized by extensive pseudopalisading necrosis, a hallmark linked to therapeutic resistance and dismal prognosis. While traditionally viewed as a passive ischemic event, the precise radiogenomic drivers and spatial immune architectures orchestrating active tumor necrosis remain poorly understood. MethodsWe integrated macroscopic clinical MRI radiomics with public genomic datasets (n=3,639), single-cell spatial transcriptomics, and high-resolution protein immunofluorescence (IF) assays in a novel co-mutant murine model to map the necrotic microenvironment. ResultsRadiomic analysis of patient MRIs demonstrated that high tumoral necrotic volume serves as a powerful independent biomarker for poor long-term survival. This macro-structural necrosis phenotype is radiogenomically driven by cell-intrinsic TP53, PTEN, and NF1 (PPN) co-mutations. Spatial transcriptomic profiling of PPN-deficient tumors revealed distinct cellular topography, separating a proliferative, invasive niche (EGFR+ SOX+, TypeInv) from a hyper-aggressive necrotic niche (ERBB3+, TypeNec). Mechanistically, TypeNec cells deploy a prominent CCL5/CXCL2 chemokine milieu that actively recruits and prompts tumor-associated neutrophils to undergo neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation. This overactive neutrophil infiltrate drives a feed-forward loop of intrinsic tumor necroptosis mediated by the release of the damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) protein HMGB2. This cascade could be therapeutically dismantled using targeted anti-inflammatory compounds. Finally, multi-cohort clinical validation confirmed that an HMGB2high signature dictates a high-risk, myeloid-rich immunosuppressive microenvironment in glioblastoma patients. ConclusionsOur findings redefine glioblastoma necrosis as an active, mutation-driven immunopathological process. The HMGB2-mediated DAMP necroptosis cascade and associated myeloid chemokines provide robust prognostic biomarkers and immediate therapeutic vulnerabilities to disrupt the immunosuppressive necrotic niche. C_LIO_LIGenomic Orchestration of Necrosis: Cross-species modeling identifies a high-risk somatic PPN co-mutation profile yielding two topographically distinct niches: an invasive niche EGFR+ SOX+, TypeInv) from a hyper-aggressive necrotic niche (ERBB3+, TypeNec). C_LIO_LIVascular Loop and DAMP Cascade: TypeNec cells deploy a CCL5/CXCL2 chemokine milieu driving perivascular neutrophil recruitment and MPO+CitH3+ NETosis, sparking a feed-forward loop of hypoxia and necrosis driven by tumor-derived HMGB2high that is pharmacologically targetable. C_LI Importance of the StudyTumor necrosis is a hallmark diagnostic feature of glioblastoma, historically characterized as a passive consequence of local tissue ischemia. This study redefines glioblastoma necrosis as an active, genetically driven immunopathological process. By integrating macroscopic clinical MRI radiomics from over 1,000 patients with single-cell spatial transcriptomics and a novel co-mutant mouse model, we reveal that cell-intrinsic TP53, PTEN, and NF1 co-mutations actively dictate a hyper-aggressive necrotic niche. Mechanistically, these mutated tumor cells deploy a CCL5/CXCL2 chemokine cascade to recruit neutrophils, triggering an overactive neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) and a HMGB2-mediated damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) loop that accelerates tissue destruction and myeloid immunosuppression. Crucially, we demonstrate that this pathogenic axis can be tracked non-invasively via standard neuroimaging and pharmacologically dismantled with anti-inflammatory small molecules, providing immediate diagnostic stratifications and a brand-new therapeutic vulnerability to disrupt the glioblastoma microenvironment. Lay SummaryDead tissue zones inside glioblastoma brain tumors, known as necrosis, are tied to poor patient survival. While long believed to be an accidental result of rapid tumor growth cutting off oxygen, this study reveals that tumor cells actively trigger this cell death. Driven by specific genetic mutations, these cells release distress signals that recruit immune cells called neutrophils. These neutrophils create a destructive, inflammatory loop that worsens the disease. By combining patient MRI scans with advanced spatial tissue mapping, we show that this destructive process can be tracked non-invasively and stopped using anti-inflammatory drugs, offering a new treatment strategy.

infographic.key_insight: Glioblastoma necrosis may be an active, mutation-driven process in which tumor-recruited neutrophils form extracellular traps and amplify HMGB2-linked tumor necroptosis.
infographic.clinical_relevance: MRI-measured necrosis and high HMGB2 expression may help identify high-risk glioblastoma, while the inflammatory cascade offers investigational therapeutic targets.
method: Integrated clinical MRI radiomics with public genomic datasets.
Mapped tumor niches using single-cell spatial transcriptomics.
Examined mechanisms using protein immunofluorescence in a TP53/PTEN/NF1 co-mutant mouse model.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports public genomic datasets totaling n=3,639, associations between MRI necrotic volume and poorer survival, and multi-cohort clinical validation of an HMGB2-high risk signature.
infographic.watch_item: Mechanistic and treatment findings are preclinical; prospective validation is needed before using these biomarkers or targets in patient care.
